job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Yara Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in cybersecurity. Mornings are lectures and a lab where we try to break into our own test networks. Afternoons I do small security checks for shops and a dentist in town, for forty or fifty pounds each, and on Saturdays I help my uncle Rafael run a phone repair stall at the market. I live in student housing in Wexcombe, and I send my mother a little money when I can. I use AI tools every day, for scanning code, writing reports and learning new attacks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, let's be sensible. Some automation will help small firms, and that's good for business. I'd tell people to learn useful skills, work hard and not wait for rescue. Then I'd get on with my lab report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's okay for me, but not safe. I have a heavy loan and about a week of costs saved, and I'm sending money home. Not many security jobs are near Wexcombe, and the bank where I interned, Marlowe Savings, only takes a couple of graduates each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and apply to Marlowe and thirty other firms, banks, consultancies and a big retailer. I'd keep doing the small checks for local businesses, and I'd try to raise my price to seventy pounds. I'd also keep Saturdays at my uncle's stall, because it's reliable money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly good. I like working, and I like earning my own way. The only knot is my mother and my little brother Tomas, who is fifteen and wants to study. I'd feel responsible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You send money to your mother. How does that affect what you can do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They've been around for six months and I have eight regular clients. If they stopped, I'd lose around two hundred a month, which is my rent share. I'd shift to the stall for more days and ask Marlowe about a contract role. I'd rather work than ask for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the small security jobs dry up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's small. About a hundred a month, and sometimes nothing. But my mother says every pound counts, and she keeps a little tin for Tomas's school books. I'd feel lousy if I couldn't add to it.

say: I'd say **sensible** automation helps small firms, and people should learn useful skills and not wait for rescue.
I'd get on with my lab report and **not make a fuss**.
think: It's okay but **not safe**: a heavy loan, a week of costs saved and money sent home.
Marlowe Savings takes only **a couple of graduates** each year.
do: Apply to **Marlowe** and thirty other banks, consultancies and retailers.
Keep the **small checks** and raise my price to seventy pounds.
Keep Saturdays at my uncle's **market stall** for reliable cash.
feel: **Fairly good**, with a knot for my mother and my brother Tomas.
S0.quote: I'd rather work than ask for help.
fieldNote: Independent streak: earns through **side work** and sends money home.
Adaptive and a daily AI user, so a plateau changes little in her day.
Family duty toward her mother and brother keeps her anxious about the loan.

Keep working Saturdays at my uncle's phone repair stall
Send my mother a fixed amount each month for Tomas's books

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good time to be useful. Companies will need people who can check the machines, and the ones who adapt will do well. I'd tell people not to complain, but to learn something that holds up. I'd also say employers should give graduates a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm optimistic but wary. Entry-level security work, like log reading and basic scanning, goes to tools, and firms might hire fewer juniors. But there will be more attacks, made faster by AI, and people to check and respond. I just need to get through the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go further with AI tools, learning how to use them for defence and how attackers use them. I'd take a cloud security certification, because every firm moves to the cloud. I'd also pitch my small business services as a package to the local business association, with a monthly fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, with some nerves. It's like a gym session: tiring, but good for you. I'd feel better if I had a contract in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Security is a field where AI helps both sides. How does that play out for a new graduate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The easy stuff, like reading logs and basic scans, goes to tools. What stays is judgement: knowing whether the alert is real, explaining it to a manager and deciding what to do. That's what I'd offer to firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to study something he's curious about and not to be scared of the tools. And to pick a skill with people in it, like teaching or care, plus one with computers. He'd roll his eyes, but he'd remember.

say: I'd say companies will need **people who can check** the machines, and those who adapt will do well.
I'd say employers should give graduates a **real chance**.
think: Basic scanning and log reading go to tools, but AI-driven attacks create **more work** for people who respond.
I just need to **get through the gate** to my first role.
do: Learn how to use AI tools for **defence** and study how attackers use them.
Pitch a **monthly package** to the local business association.
feel: **Energised with nerves**, like a hard gym session that's good for you.
S1.quote: What stays is judgement: knowing whether the alert is real, explaining it to a manager and deciding what to do.
fieldNote: Sees her field as **two-sided**: AI automates defence tasks and creates new threats.
Her answer is to sell judgement and a monthly service.
Advice to her brother mixes people skills with computing.

steps.text: Study how attackers use AI tools and how to defend against them
Pitch a monthly security package to the local business association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should not panic, but they should be ready to help each other. Churches, families and neighbours matter most when systems fail. I'd say we need practical help: food, rent and retraining, run close to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's scary. By 2028 AI does most thinking work, including most of what I'd do in cybersecurity. I'd graduate in the middle of it, and the work left would be risk and responsibility, which firms might hand to a few experienced people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use my side work as my base: more small clients, more days at the stall, a few more hours online. I'd go for any role where a person is accountable, like incident response or compliance. And I'd keep my AI skills sharp, because someone has to run the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I wouldn't freeze. I'd feel the loan and my mother's tin pressing on me. I'd work more and sleep less, which is how I handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What do you do when your skills are the thing that's replaced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be straight: things are tight, I'll send what I can and I'll move home if I have to. She'd say no, don't give up your life. But she'd also make me a pot of stew, and I'd be okay for a night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you talk to your mother about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might start a small shop of my own, doing security and computer repair for families and shops. It's not glamorous, but there's a local need, and the big firms don't want that work. I'd be the person on the high street.

say: I'd say people should **not panic** but be ready to help each other, because churches and families matter most when systems fail.
I'd ask for **practical help** like food, rent and retraining, run close to people.
think: By 2028 AI does most **thinking work**, including most of what I'd do in security.
What remains is **risk and responsibility**, which firms might give to a few experienced people.
do: Build more **small clients** and add days at the stall.
Aim for roles where a **person is accountable**, like incident response.
Be straight with my **mother** and move home if I must.
feel: **Alarmed but not frozen**, working more and sleeping less.
S2.quote: I might start a small shop of my own, doing security and computer repair for families and shops.
fieldNote: Her adaptive streak turns fear into a **small-business plan**.

Still anxious rather than alarmed: she has income streams and skills.

steps.text: Add more small clients and more days at the repair stall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people act now. I'd say schools should teach people how to use these systems, firms should hire and train, and churches and communities should check on those who struggle. And government shouldn't get in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel capable. By 2031 I'd have a job, some of the loan paid and a savings pot. The work will change, but I'd have a head start because I'm already using the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a security job, keep the side clients on the weekends and put money into the stall to make it a proper repair shop. I'd use the tools to automate my own reports, so I'd do more in less time. And I'd save a third of everything I earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, with a bit of fear around the edge. It's like climbing a hill in fog. I can't see the top, but I can see the next stone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What does the extra time let you do that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me pick a job rather than grabbing whatever there is. I could choose a firm that's investing in people, learn its systems and start a small business of my own on the side. Two years is too short for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your family in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd send more money home and help Tomas apply to university. By then he'd be about twenty, so I'd be able to pay for his first year. That would feel like something real.

say: I'd say schools should **teach** these systems and firms should hire and train.
I'd say churches and communities should **check on** those who struggle.
think: I feel capable, with a job, some of the loan paid and a **savings pot** by 2031.
I have a **head start** because I already use the tools.

steps.text: Take a security job and keep side clients on weekends
Put money into the stall and grow it into a repair shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time, so let's rebuild: apprenticeships, small firms and local support, with people helping their neighbours. I'd tell young people to start something of their own, because ten years is long enough to grow a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm confident. I'd have a career, a small shop and the loan gone. The change comes, but I'd have used the decade to grow in the middle, between the tools and the people who need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for a firm for about three years, then go out on my own with a small security and repair business. I'd hire Tomas or a cousin for the shop. And I'd buy a flat in Wexcombe, or help my mother get one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit giddy, honestly. I'd still check the news at night, but only to know what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What does a good outcome look like for you and your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably both for a while. The job teaches me how big firms work, and the stall keeps me connected to the street. In ten years I'd want the shop to be what pays and the firm to be where I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still keep both the job and the stall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother in a flat that's hers, Tomas finished with university and a business with my name on it. And the church choir, since my grandmother would like to hear me sing.

say: I'd say ten years is long enough to **grow a business**, so young people should start something of their own.
I'd say we should rebuild **local support**, with neighbours helping each other.
think: I'm confident: a career, a small shop and the **loan gone** by then.
I'd grow in the middle, between the tools and **people who need them**.
do: Work at a firm for about **three years**, then start my own security and repair business.
**Hire** Tomas or a cousin for the shop.

S4.quote: In ten years I'd want the shop to be what pays and the firm to be where I learn.

steps.text: Work at a security firm for three years, then open my own business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits just as my family needs me most. What would help is small-business support, so people like me can build a shop, and training that teaches people to use these systems, not just fear them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'm proud of. I'm proud that my mother's tin for Tomas's books has my name on a few of the pounds in it. It isn't much, but it's mine, and I earned it.

headlineQuote: I'm proud that my mother's tin for Tomas's books has my name on a few of the pounds in it.
portrait: Yara is a **24-year-old** top computing graduate doing a master's in cybersecurity, in student housing in Wexcombe, with a heavy loan.
She uses AI tools **every day** and earns from small security checks and her uncle's phone repair stall.
She holds traditional views: family, faith, **community** and earning your own way.
She sends money to her mother and aims to pay for her brother Tomas's study.
Her mood is **anxious** in most worlds and only uneasy with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because it comes just when her family needs her income.
whatWouldHelp: **Small-business support** and training that teaches people to use these systems, not just fear them.
